paper_metadata.title: Hybrid Photonic Quantum Reservoir Computing for High-Dimensional Financial Surface Prediction

summary: The paper proposes a hybrid photonic quantum reservoir computing pipeline for swaption surface prediction, combining 1,215 Fock-basis features from three photonic reservoirs with a Ridge readout. On a dataset of 494 daily surfaces with 6 held-out test days, the method achieves the best surface RMSE of 0.0425, slightly outperforming classical LSTM (0.0445) but with statistically insignificant differences; variational quantum models perform poorly with negative R² values (-1.089 and -1.306).

experiments.description: Fixed photonic quantum reservoir computing ensemble with three photonic reservoirs and Ridge regression readout for swaption surface prediction.

algorithm.variant: photonic quantum reservoir computing (QORC) ensemble with fixed reservoirs and Ridge readout
algorithm.optimizer: Ridge regression (closed-form); no trainable quantum optimizer
algorithm.convergence_criteria: closed-form Ridge solution; no iterative quantum training
algorithm.parameter_initialization: Reservoir unitaries are Haar-random and fixed after initialization; phase encoding uses a fixed orthogonal projection with sigmoid mapping

problem_formulation.encoding_details: 120-dimensional classical context is projected to photonic phases via a fixed orthogonal map W and sigmoid, then encoded as phases phi_i = 2π·σ(Wx); Fock-basis probabilities are measured from fixed linear-optical circuits
problem_formulation.objective_function: Predict next-day 20-dimensional latent code z_{t+1} from a 5-step window of latent codes and first-difference momentum, then decode to 224-dimensional swaption surface; Ridge minimizes ||z_{t+1} - Wf_t - b||^2_2 + α||W||^2_F

problem_instance.description: Next-day prediction of high-dimensional swaption surfaces from historical daily market data

dataset_specification.description: 494 daily swaption surfaces, each 224-dimensional (14×16 tenor-maturity grid); 6 future days held out for test

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Three-stage preprocessing: winsorization at 1st/99th percentiles on training data, robust scaling by median and IQR, then min-max normalization to [0,1]; sparse denoising autoencoder compresses 224→20 with 15% random masking during training; temporal windowing with k=5 and first-difference momentum
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Single train/validation/test split with 439 training windows, last 50 windows for validation, and 6 future days for walk-forward test; metrics reported on held-out test set

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Winsorization, robust scaling, min-max normalization, sparse denoising autoencoder, temporal windowing
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Ridge output decoded by autoencoder decoder back to 224-dimensional surface; inverse preprocessing applied to return to original price scale

speedup_claims.factor: 2.2x lower latent MSE than QUANTECH MLP
speedup_claims.conditions: same 1,215-dimensional QORC features; test set of 6 held-out days
speedup_claims.caveats: This is an accuracy comparison, not a runtime speedup.

speedup_claims.factor: 0.10 ms/sample inference, 0.06 ms slower than classical Ridge but faster than all other non-Ridge baselines
speedup_claims.caveats: Reported latencies exclude quantum feature extraction; paper notes circuits were classically simulated.
Paper states classical simulation scales as O((n+m-1 choose n)); no asymptotic advantage is proven.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: Classical simulation of Fock probabilities scales as O( (n+m-1 choose n) ) in the paper's discussion; photonic hardware measures output click patterns at optical speed
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: O( (n+m-1 choose n) ) for classical simulation of Fock probabilities

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Larger photonic reservoirs with photon numbers beyond classical simulation limits
limiting_factors: All experiments performed via classical photonic simulation
Performance differences among top models not statistically significant due to only 6 test samples
No demonstrated runtime or accuracy advantage over classical baselines

notes: Paper reports photonic reservoirs implemented with Perceval/MerLin and fixed linear-optical circuits, but does not specify a qubit count; num_qubits is not directly applicable to the photonic Fock-state model and is left null.
Circuit depth is not reported for the photonic reservoirs; only the sandwich architecture U_rand · PS(phi) · U_rand is described.

Hardware.type set to real_qpu_photonic because the paper frames the method as photonic quantum computing, though it also states all circuits were classically simulated in limitations; the experimental setup itself is photonic rather than a gate-based simulator/QPU benchmark.
Authors do not claim quantum advantage; they report best surface RMSE (0.0425) but acknowledge differences among top models are within noise given small test set.
